items.answer: Interaction is the activity that takes place between a user and a system, often by manipulating an image or parts of it with input devices. In immersive environments it is broadly categorized into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

Degree of freedom is an indication of the different ways an object can move in space; in 3D space, an object can have six degrees of freedom: three translational degrees of freedom along the x, y, and z axes, and three rotational degrees of freedom called yaw, roll, and pitch.

items.prompt: What is six degrees of freedom?
items.answer: Six degrees of freedom is the total of six freedoms an object can have in three-dimensional space, consisting of three rotational freedoms called yaw, roll, and pitch, and three translational freedoms along the x, y, and z axes.

Object interaction is a kind of interaction in immersive virtual environments that involves selecting one or more virtual objects in the environment and manipulating a selected object to change its properties.

Navigation is an interaction in an immersive virtual world that moves the user from one point to another by changing the user's viewpoint, mostly without object interaction, and has two components: locomotion and wayfinding.

An augmented reality system is a system with four required characteristics: it enhances the real world with computer-generated digital content registered in 3D, that content is experienced through the user's sensory organs, and it supports real-time interaction with that content in the enhanced environment.

questions.question: Which interaction category is used to initialize parameters and set options in an immersive experience?
options: Navigation
Object interaction
System control
Object selection
questions.explanation: System control is the interaction category for setting up the experience, such as initializing parameters and selecting options. Object interaction and navigation deal with virtual objects and movement, not setup.

data.text: Interaction in immersive experience design is grouped into three broad categories. Object interaction involves interacting with virtual objects, while navigation moves from one point to another with a corresponding change in viewpoint; it mostly does not involve object interaction, though some navigation techniques may require it. System control is set apart from object manipulation, object interaction, and navigation; it is a mostly regular type of interaction used to set up the system, initialize parameters, provide initial information, and set options or menus.
points: Interaction in immersive experience design is broadly divided into object interaction, navigation, and system control.

questions.question: In virtual environments, how do selection and manipulation of objects differ?
options: Selection changes a target, while manipulation chooses the target object
Selection moves the camera, while manipulation changes the target object
Selection identifies a scene, while manipulation chooses the target object
Selection chooses a target, while manipulation changes the chosen object
questions.explanation: Selection specifies one or more objects from the virtual world, while manipulation interacts with a selected object to change its properties. Moving the camera is navigation, not object selection.

questions.question: Why do target distance, size, density, direction, and number of targets matter when choosing an object selection technique?
options: They can define what sensory stimulus is needed for the selection task
They can determine how much latency is needed for the selection task
They can set which surface material is used for the selection task
They can influence how well a user completes the selection task
questions.explanation: These variables are important because they affect user performance in the selection task, helping a designer choose a technique that maximizes selection performance. They are not primarily about latency, sensory stimulus type, or surface material.

questions.question: Before a fully occluded virtual object can be selected, what has to be true for the user?
options: The user has to be able to point at it
The user has to be made aware of it
The user has to be able to move it
The user has to be able to see it
questions.explanation: A fully occluded object may still be selectable, but the user first has to be told or otherwise made aware that it is there. Seeing, pointing, or moving it are not the required first step for a fully hidden target.

data.text: Object interaction in virtual experiences separates selection from manipulation, and the explanation concentrates on selecting virtual objects. Selection performance depends on viewpoint distance, direction, target size, surrounding density, and number of targets, while occlusion can create special difficulties. The techniques considered are hand, pointing-based, image plane, volume-based, and bimanual selection.
points: Virtual object interaction includes selection, which specifies objects, and manipulation, which changes selected object properties; they mostly use separate techniques.
Selection technique choice depends on viewpoint distance, direction, target size, surrounding density, and number of targets to maximize performance.
Target occlusion can affect selection: partially occluded targets can need specialized techniques, and fully occluded targets require user awareness.
Object selection techniques include hand, pointing-based, image plane, volume-based, and bimanual selection.

questions.question: Why can the virtual hand technique become annoying when the selected object is far away?
options: The physical hand must stop for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
The virtual arm must lengthen for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
The physical hand must move for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
The proximity sphere must shrink for a long time before the virtual grab occurs
questions.explanation: The virtual hand follows the physical hand closely, so reaching a distant object can require a long real hand movement. The other options describe effects of other techniques, not the basic virtual hand.

questions.question: How does the go-go technique make a distant virtual object easier to reach?
options: It maps smaller physical hand movements to the same virtual hand movements as distance grows
It maps smaller physical hand movements to slower virtual hand movements as distance grows
It maps smaller physical hand movements to stopped virtual hand movements as distance grows
It maps smaller physical hand movements to faster virtual hand movements as distance grows
questions.explanation: Go-go increases virtual hand movement for smaller physical hand movements as the target gets farther, reducing the real movement needed to reach it. A one-to-one or reduced mapping would not provide that reaching benefit.

questions.question: What control does the prism technique add for a distant target that go-go does not have?
options: Stopping the physical hand can enlarge the proximity sphere
Stopping the physical hand can shorten the virtual arm
Stopping the physical hand can stop the virtual hand
Stopping the physical hand can lengthen the virtual arm
questions.explanation: Prism can keep the virtual hand still when the physical hand is still, which helps with precise distant selection. Go-go lacks that stop control, and stopping does not change arm length or the proximity sphere.

questions.question: In intent-driven selection, what does the posture of the virtual fingers indicate?
options: The user's finger position around an object
The user's confidence in selecting an object
The user's physical distance from an object
The user's physical speed toward an object
questions.explanation: Finger posture expresses the user's confidence in the intended target, helping refine the selection. It is not a measure of physical distance, physical speed, or the finger position itself.

data.text: Hand-based object selection uses the physical hand to virtually touch and grab objects. Its techniques differ in reach: virtual hand keeps a one-to-one avatar of the physical hand but can make distant reaches tiring, while go-go and prism adjust speed for distant objects and introduce precision, stopping, and alignment trade-offs. Intent-driven selection refines a target through finger posture and shrinking proximity spheres, and it can be combined with the go-go or prism travel techniques.
points: Hand selection uses one physical hand to virtually touch and grab objects, with virtual hand, go-go, prism, and intent-driven techniques.
Virtual hand maps the physical hand one-to-one to a visible hand, but distant objects require tiring reaches.
Go-go speeds distant reaches but loses precision, while prism improves go-go by slowing or stopping the hand, but mismatches positions.
Intent-driven selection uses finger posture and shrinking proximity spheres to indicate confidence and refine the chosen object.
Go-go and prism are travel techniques, while intent-driven selection is a grabbing technique that can combine with them.

questions.question: How does the display-based non-hand pointing method place and move the virtual ray?
options: It places the ray at the head position and moves it with head movement
It places the ray at the depth marker position and moves it with hand movement
It places the ray at the eye position and moves it with gaze movement
It places the ray at the controller position and moves it with hand movement
questions.explanation: The non-hand pointing method that uses a head-mounted display places the ray at the head and moves it with head movement. Eye-gaze, hand, and depth-marker movement are different pointing or selection mechanisms.

questions.question: Why is a small distant object hard to select with basic ray casting?
options: A depth marker selects the object closest to it
The virtual ray must be aimed at the object precisely
The virtual ray bends toward the closest selectable object
The head-mounted display moves the ray with eye movement
questions.explanation: Basic ray casting selects the first object intersected by the ray, so a small distant target demands precise aiming, especially when nearby objects compete for that intersection. Bending the ray is bend cast, and a depth marker belongs to depth ray.

questions.question: What does the improvement that calculates point-line distance do in pointing-based selection?
options: It places a depth marker near the intended object
It selects the first intersected object
It curves the ray toward the closest selectable object
It uses eye gaze to estimate the intended object
questions.explanation: The point-line-distance improvement is the one that curves the ray toward the closest selectable object, reducing the need for exact aiming. Selecting the first intersected object is basic ray casting, a depth marker is depth ray, and gaze estimation is a different pointing method.

questions.question: When does bend cast work best?
options: When many objects are near the ray's path at similar distances
When the user points with the eye instead of the hand
When the intended object is closest to a user-controlled depth marker
When only a few objects are near the ray's path
questions.explanation: Bend cast chooses the closest selectable object, so it works best when few objects are near the ray and the intended object is likely the closest. Many nearby objects with similar distances can make the intended object not be the closest, and depth markers or eye pointing are different methods.

questions.question: How does the marker-based improvement to basic ray casting disambiguate multiple intersected objects?
options: It lets the user move a marker and select the intersected object closest to it
It lets the user move a marker and select the farthest intersected object
It lets the user move a marker and select the largest intersected object
It lets the user move a marker and select the first intersected object
questions.explanation: The marker-based improvement lets the user position a marker along the pointing direction and select the intersected object closest to that marker. Selecting the first, farthest, or largest intersected object does not use the marker to resolve ambiguity.

data.text: Pointing-based selection uses a visible ray from a hand, head, or eye, with a trigger selecting the first intersected object. The ray may be short or infinite, and gaze can aim while the hand triggers. Ray casting is basic but can be imprecise for small distant objects, so bend cast bends the ray toward a closest object when few are nearby, and depth ray uses a depth marker to choose among intersected objects.
points: Pointing-based selection uses a visible ray and a controller trigger to select the first object it hits.
Pointing-based selection uses a short or infinite ray from a hand, head, or eye; sometimes gaze aims and hand triggers.
Ray casting is basic ray pointing, but small distant objects are harder to select precisely among others.
Bend cast bends the ray to the closest selectable object, reducing aiming precision, but works best with few nearby objects.
Depth ray adds a hand-positioned depth marker to choose the intersected object closest to that marker.

questions.question: In image-plane selection, what does the user hold between the eye and the desired object?
options: A virtual cone cast from a hand
One or two hands or fingers
A virtual sphere cast onto a surface
A virtual ray cast from the eye
questions.explanation: Image-plane selection uses the user's hands or fingers as the element between the eye and the object. Rays, cones, and spheres belong to other selection ideas.

questions.question: Compared with image-plane selection, what does volumetric selection allow the user to select?
options: The first object intersected by a ray
An object aligned with a hand or finger
An object on a two-dimensional view plane
A three-dimensional region
questions.explanation: Volumetric selection selects objects inside a 3D region, while image-plane selection operates on a 2D view plane and ray casting targets the first intersected object.

questions.question: In the two-handed box selection technique, what do both hands progressively reduce?
options: A sphere
A frame
A cone
A box
questions.explanation: Two-handed box selection uses both hands to position, orient, and shape a box, then reduces it to isolate a region of 3D space. Cones, spheres, and frames describe other selection techniques.

questions.question: What makes small-object selection harder when a volumetric technique is used in a complex virtual environment?
options: A sparse layout in the environment
Many objects in the environment
One object in the environment
A less precise aim in the environment
questions.explanation: Volumetric selection selects objects inside its 3D region, so a complex scene with many objects makes it hard to isolate a small target. Isolation, sparsity, and aiming precision describe easier cases or other techniques.

data.text: Image-plane and volumetric selection form the third category of object selection. Image-plane methods select on a two-dimensional view plane by occlusion or framing, while volumetric methods select objects inside a three-dimensional region using cone, sphere, or two-handed box methods. Volumetric methods can pick multiple objects, and they are most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in less complex virtual environments.
points: The third object selection category is image-plane or volumetric selection.
Image-plane selection is 2D occlusion/framing: the user aligns a hand or finger with an object and signals.
Image-plane techniques include head crusher, sticky finger, lifting palm, and framing hands, with framing hands being more common.
Volumetric selection selects objects inside a 3D region using cone, sphere, or two-handed box methods; cones can select multiple objects.
Volumetric selection is most useful for small, well-defined isolated objects in less complex virtual environments.

questions.question: What does object manipulation usually mean in an XR interaction?
options: Changing object properties after selection
Correcting drift in the object's position
Tracking the pose of the object in space
Selecting the desired object from a 2D view plane
questions.explanation: Object manipulation modifies an object's properties such as position, orientation, scale, or texture, and it typically follows selection. Selecting, pose tracking, and drift correction are separate interaction or tracking steps.

questions.question: What does hand manipulation use to act on objects?
options: A cone cast toward the object
A pair of hands framing the object
A ray cast from the user toward the object
A hand representation acting on the object
questions.explanation: Hand manipulation extends the virtual hand idea by using a virtual hand to manipulate the object. Ray casting, cone casting, and framing hands are selection techniques rather than the core idea of hand manipulation.

questions.question: What is a likely trade-off of hand-based manipulation in XR?
options: The need for more processing or costlier hardware
The need for tracking the user's sense organs
The need for selecting objects in a 3D region
The need for estimating the user's initial registration
questions.explanation: Hand manipulation can require more computational power or specialized devices, which may be relatively costly. Registration, volumetric selection, and sense-organ tracking are separate XR concerns.

data.text: Object manipulation changes an object's properties, usually after the object has been selected. Several manipulation techniques exist: hand, indirect, bimanual, and integrated hybrid. Hand manipulation is the first such technique: it uses a virtual hand after hand selection, with smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controllers; it is the most intuitive way, though it may need somewhat more computational power or specialized devices that may be relatively costly.
points: Object manipulation modifies an object's properties and usually comes after selecting that object.
Object manipulation techniques include hand, indirect, bimanual, and integrated hybrid manipulation.
Hand manipulation uses a virtual hand after hand selection, with smart gloves, gesture-based manipulation, or controllers, and is most intuitive.
Hand manipulation may need somewhat more computational power or specialized devices that may be relatively costly.

questions.question: In an indirect object-manipulation technique, how does the user's physical hand affect a virtual object?
options: By moving a separate object that is mapped to it
By moving both controllers symmetrically around it
By moving a virtual hand that reaches it
By framing it on a view plane
questions.explanation: Indirect manipulation works through intermediary objects that are mapped to the target, so the user moves a mapped object rather than the target itself. A virtual hand or bimanual controllers act on the target or through a different direct/bimanual technique, and framing on a view plane is a selection method.

questions.question: Why can several 3D widgets be needed for one virtual object?
options: Because each widget is linked to a separate physical prop for the object
Because each widget handles a small set of degrees of freedom for the object
Because each widget requires a separate image-plane selection of the object
Because each widget represents a separate miniature model of the whole object
questions.explanation: A 3D widget is usually responsible for only a small set of manipulation degrees of freedom, so different widgets may be used for different object properties. Miniature models, physical props, and image-plane selection belong to other techniques or to selection rather than to the normal reason for using multiple widgets.

questions.question: What does the user move in the indirect grasping method that feels more natural?
options: A physical prop linked to the target object
A view plane in front of the user
A virtual hand placed in the scene
A miniature model of the whole environment
questions.explanation: The more natural indirect grasping method lets the user move a physical prop that is linked to the target, so the prop's movement moves the linked virtual object. A miniature model is a different world-in-miniature arrangement, while a virtual hand and a view plane belong to other manipulation or selection ideas.

questions.question: For a distant object, what does a small handheld model of the virtual environment let the user do?
options: Move the whole virtual environment around in that model
Reach the distant virtual object's body in that model
Select the distant virtual object itself in that model
Manipulate the object's representation in that model
questions.explanation: A world-in-miniature model represents objects in a small handheld form, so a distant object can be acted on through its representation without reaching or selecting the distant object itself. The model is not used to move the entire environment, and it does not require the user to reach the object by hand.

questions.question: Why is a small handheld model of the virtual environment difficult to use for a large and complex world?
options: Because moving both hands together for it is very difficult
Because linking a physical prop to it is very difficult
Because making that model for such a world is very difficult
Because selecting objects outside reach in it is very difficult
questions.explanation: The practical problem for large and complex environments is that creating the handheld miniature model is very difficult. The other options describe difficulties associated with selection, bimanual synchronization, or physical-proxy linking, not with building the model itself.

data.text: Indirect manipulation controls virtual objects through other mapped objects rather than by moving the virtual object with the physical hand. One simple form uses 3D widgets placed in the scene, although each usually handles only a small set of degrees of freedom. Proxy-based techniques let a user move a local proxy to move a linked virtual object, and world-in-miniature uses a handheld miniature model to reach objects both nearby and distant, though building that model is hard for large complex environments.
points: Indirect manipulation controls virtual objects by manipulating mapped objects, not by manipulating the virtual objects with the physical hand.
3D widgets are scene controls; each typically handles a small set of degrees of freedom, so several may be used.
Indirect proxies offer more natural grasping by letting users move a local proxy that moves a linked virtual object.
World-in-miniature is a miniature proxy model, where manipulating a model object moves the corresponding virtual object, both nearby and distant.
World-in-miniature is not very practical for large, complex virtual environments because making its miniature model is very difficult.

questions.question: In the spindle technique, how are the two handheld controllers positioned?
options: symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis
on the same side of an imaginary axis
asymmetrically around an imaginary axis
at arbitrary points around the same imaginary axis
questions.explanation: The spindle technique defines a virtual spindle by placing two handheld controllers symmetrically on both sides of an imaginary axis. Asymmetric or arbitrary placement is not part of the basic spindle technique.

questions.question: Why can the spindle technique require a lot of practice?
options: Asymmetric hand movement
Asynchronous hand movement
Single-controller hand movement
Synchronous hand movement
questions.explanation: The spindle technique can be hard to use efficiently because it requires the two hands to move synchronously while interacting. Asynchronous movement is a different bimanual pattern, and spindle uses two controllers rather than one.

questions.question: Which property do the spindle and spindle plus wheel techniques both keep?
options: synchronous hand movement
asynchronous hand movement
manipulation through a miniature model
symmetric hand placement around an imaginary axis
questions.explanation: Both spindle and spindle plus wheel require the hands to be moved together, so they are synchronous techniques. Symmetric hand placement applies to spindle, not necessarily to spindle plus wheel, and miniature-model manipulation is a different indirect technique.

data.text: Bimanual manipulation techniques use both hands, and their movement may be synchronous or asynchronous. The spindle technique is a symmetric synchronous form in which two handheld six-degree-of-freedom controllers define a virtual spindle, allowing a virtual world object to be moved or rotated by unison hand movement. Because it requires synchronized movement, it needs practice to use efficiently, while spindle plus wheel relaxes the symmetry requirement while keeping the hands synchronous.
points: A bimanual manipulation technique uses both hands, with synchronous or asynchronous hand movement.
The spindle technique uses two symmetrically placed, simultaneously moved six-degree-of-freedom handheld controllers around an imaginary axis.
In the spindle technique, unison hand movement can move and also simultaneously rotate a virtual world object.
The spindle technique is not easy because synchronous hand movement in a virtual world requires practice to use efficiently.
Spindle plus wheel is an asymmetric synchronous extension of the spindle technique, requiring both hands moved together but not symmetrically.

questions.question: In an integrated hybrid manipulation technique, what is the next automatic transition after the user selects an object?
options: A return to selection mode
A user request for manipulation mode
A switch to manipulation mode
A wait in selection mode
questions.explanation: Integrated hybrid manipulation automatically switches from selection to manipulation after selection, without an explicit user signal. A return to selection mode happens later, after manipulation, not as the next transition after selection.

questions.question: In HOMER, which part is moved to the selected object when the ray intersects it?
options: The physical controller is moved to the object
The ray is moved to the object
The virtual hand is moved to the object
The selection cursor is moved to the object
questions.explanation: In HOMER, the virtual hand automatically moves to the object and attaches to it when the ray intersects the desired object. The ray is the pointing element, but it is not the part that attaches to the object.

questions.question: In HOMER, what ends the manipulation of an object?
options: A pause in continuous hand movement for a while acts as the signal
A loss of ray contact with the selected object acts as the signal
A change in the object pose in the scene acts as the signal
A trigger or a specific hand gesture acts as the signal
questions.explanation: Manipulation in HOMER ends when the user indicates that the manipulation job is done through a trigger or a specific hand gesture, after which the virtual hand returns to its original position.

data.text: Integrated hybrid manipulation describes techniques that automatically move from selection to manipulation and back without an explicit user signal. HOMER applies this idea by combining ray-casting selection with hand manipulation. When the ray selects an object, HOMER attaches the user's virtual hand to the object, enables hand manipulation of its position and orientation, and ends with a trigger or specific gesture that returns the hand to its original position.
points: Integrated hybrid manipulation techniques automatically switch from selection to manipulation and back without an explicit user signal.
HOMER is an integrated hybrid technique that combines ray-casting selection with hand manipulation, so they are not separate.
In HOMER, when the ray hits the desired object, the virtual hand automatically attaches, not the ray.
After the virtual hand attaches, HOMER switches to manipulation mode, enabling hand manipulation of the object's position and orientation.
In HOMER, a trigger or specific hand gesture ends manipulation and returns the virtual hand to its original position.

activities.title: Order the stages of HOMER object manipulation

items.title: Order the stages of HOMER object manipulation
steps: The pointing ray intersects the object
The virtual hand attaches to the object
The virtual hand manipulates the object
The system switches to selection mode

questions.question: Why can augmented reality use regular interaction techniques while immersive environments need improved ones?
options: AR blocks the user's senses, whereas immersive environments do not block them in the ideal case
AR blocks sensory stimuli, whereas immersive environments supply them freely in the ideal case
AR depends on familiar controls, whereas immersive environments replace them in the ideal case
AR does not block the user's senses, whereas immersive environments do in the ideal case
questions.explanation: In augmented reality, the user's senses are not blocked, so ordinary interaction techniques remain usable. Immersive environments, by contrast, aim to block the senses and cut off the real world, so improved interaction techniques are needed.

questions.question: What is the common focus of object selection and object manipulation?
options: System-control window objects
Real-world physical objects
Virtual objects
Ordinary computer objects
questions.explanation: Object selection and object manipulation are interaction techniques related to virtual objects. They are not primarily about ordinary computer objects, real-world physical objects, or system-control windows.

questions.question: How do navigation techniques differ from system-control interaction?
options: Navigation selects virtual objects, while system control uses manipulation techniques
Navigation controls a computer, while system control uses movement techniques
Navigation blocks the senses, while system control uses sensory techniques
Navigation moves the user, while system control uses familiar techniques
questions.explanation: Navigation is about moving from one point to another in a virtual world, while system-control interaction mainly relies on regular techniques familiar from any computer system. Reversing these roles or mixing them with object manipulation or sensory blocking would be incorrect.

data.text: XR interaction depends on whether the user's senses remain open or are blocked. Augmented reality leaves the user's senses open, so regular techniques can address the virtual augmentation of the real world, whereas immersive environments ideally block senses and call for improved techniques. In immersive environments, object selection and manipulation concern virtual objects, while navigation covers moving through a virtual world and system control interaction covers familiar computer-system techniques.
points: Augmented reality systems can use regular interaction techniques for real-world virtual augmentation because the user's senses are not blocked.
Immersive environments ideally block the user's senses, so improved interaction techniques are needed for a better immersive experience.
Object selection and object manipulation are two interaction techniques, typically used in immersive environments, related to virtual objects.
Navigation techniques are interaction techniques for moving from one point to another in a virtual world.
System control interaction is a third category primarily relying on regular interaction techniques familiar in any computer system.

questions.question: Why might the prism technique be easier to control than the go-go technique when selecting a small distant virtual object?
questions.reference_answer: The prism technique is easier to control because slowing or stopping the physical hand slows or stops the virtual hand, which go-go cannot do. Go-go maps smaller physical movements to larger, faster virtual movements as distance increases, so a distant small target can be missed or bypassed. Prism scales down virtual motion when the hand is slow and keeps the virtual hand still below a minimum speed.

questions.question: Why might depth ray be more reliable than bend cast when several objects are close to the path of a virtual ray?
questions.reference_answer: Depth ray is more reliable in that case because the user can choose depth explicitly, while bend cast relies on closeness to the ray. Bend cast bends toward the closest selectable object by point-line distance, so several nearby objects of similar distances can make the intended object not the closest. Depth ray uses a user-controlled depth marker to disambiguate multiple intersected objects and select the one closest to the marker.

questions.question: How does Hand-Centered Object Manipulation Extending Ray Casting combine selection and manipulation into one continuous interaction?
questions.reference_answer: It reduces separate actions by automatically moving from selection to manipulation once a ray selects the object. Selection and manipulation mostly use separate techniques. HOMER mixes ray casting with hand manipulation and switches automatically without an explicit signal; when the ray intersects the object, the virtual hand moves to and attaches to it.

questions.question: Why is world in miniature less practical for large and complex virtual environments even though it can manipulate distant virtual objects?
questions.reference_answer: World in miniature becomes less practical for large and complex virtual environments because creating the miniature model is very difficult. The technique provides a miniature handheld model that represents all objects in the virtual environment. Manipulating an object in that model manipulates the corresponding actual object, even outside the user's reach, but that complete model is hard to create when the environment is large and complex.
